keyVerseText: And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew name מוֹרִיָּה (Môwrîyâh) derives from the root רָאָה (râʼâh), meaning to see, behold, or perceive, combined with the divine element יָהּ (Yah), a shortened form of Jehovah. Thus, Moriah literally means "chosen by Jehovah" or "seen by Yahweh," emphasizing divine selection and revelation. This root sense adds a dimension of God’s attentive presence and sovereign choice beyond the mere geographic designation found in English translations.
usageInScripture: The term מוֹרִיָּה appears only twice in Scripture, consistently translated as "Moriah" or "of Moriah," referring to a specific location. It denotes both the hill where Abraham was commanded to sacrifice Isaac and the mount on which Solomon built the temple, showing a strong geographical and theological consistency. The limited but focused usage highlights Moriah as a divinely appointed place of testing, sacrifice, and worship.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מוֹרִיָּה as "chosen by Jehovah" deepens our appreciation of God’s providential work in salvation history. It marks a place where God’s presence is uniquely manifested—first in Abraham’s obedience and later in the temple’s establishment. This name reminds believers that God both sees and chooses the moments and places of covenantal encounter, pointing ultimately to Christ as the perfect offering and the true temple where God’s presence dwells. It encourages faith in God’s sovereign guidance and provision even in moments of trial.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 22:2, God commands Abraham to take Isaac to the land of Moriah for sacrifice, underscoring the location’s divine appointment. The name Moriah here conveys that this is not merely a physical place but one chosen and seen by God for a profound test of faith. It highlights the trust Abraham must place in God’s provision and foreshadows the ultimate sacrifice God would provide. The word Moriah enriches the verse by anchoring it in God’s sovereign and redemptive plan.
